A deterministic offline client for tests, demos and dry runs

Source: R/core-transport-mock.R
hr_mock_client.Rd

handler receives (messages, params) and returns either a string or a gr_result. Every call is recorded in $calls(), so tests can assert on the exact prompts a strategy produced, which is how you prove two reading strategies are actually different.

Usage

hr_mock_client(handler = NULL, embed_handler = NULL, mode = NULL)

Arguments

handler

Function of (messages, params) returning a string or a gr_result.

embed_handler

Function of (texts, params) returning a numeric matrix with one row per input.

mode

NULL (the default) for replies as the handler gives them, or one of "bad_json", "refuse" and "at_cap", or a vector of HTTP status codes such as c(429, 500, 200). See Details.

Value

An object of class gr_client, with $calls(), $embeds() and $reset().

Details

Three things to know about the mock. It registers two model ids ("mock-model", "mock-embed") in the session's model registry the first time it is called, so they appear in hr_models() afterwards. Its default handler returns plain text, so readers that need JSON-schema output (rerank, iterative) take their documented degraded path unless your handler returns valid JSON for those prompts. And hr_embed() uses its embed_handler unless hr_options(embedder =) names a registered embedder (see the embedder argument of hr_embed()), reporting embedding_source = "api", so an offline run gets semantic-shaped vectors rather than the lexical fallback. A mock embed handler that fails or returns the wrong number of rows is still caught and still degrades, like any other.

mode makes the mock misbehave the way a provider can, so you can test how your code copes offline. It changes chat replies only; embeddings are left as they are.

"bad_json"

Every reply is a JSON object cut off part way, so a request with a JSON schema gets a reply that does not parse.

"refuse"

Every reply is empty, which hr_call() reports as a failed result with finish_reason = "empty", as it does a refusal from a provider.

"at_cap"

Every reply is the handler's, marked as cut off at the output cap (finish_reason = "length") and billed at the full cap. A failed gr_result from the handler comes back as it is.

A vector of HTTP status codes

Call i gets the i-th status, and every call after the last gets the last one. A status from 200 to 299 gives the handler's reply; any other gives a failed result with that status, marked retryable for the statuses the HTTP transport retries (408, 409, 425, 429, 500, 502, 503 and 504). The mock does not retry, so each status is one call. $reset() starts the sequence again.

See also

hr_client(), hr_call(), gr_result, gr_example() for a document to run against

Examples

cl <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) "mock answer")
hr_call(cl, list(list(role = "user", content = "hi")))$text
#> [1] "mock answer"

# `$calls()` is how you prove two reading strategies differ: it records the
# exact prompts each one sent.
cl$reset()
ch <- gr_segment(gr_example(), list(method = "paragraph", max_tokens = 150))
#> Using cached ingestion for this document + settings.
#> Segmenting with 'paragraph' (cap 150 tokens, overlap 0).
invisible(gr_read(ch, "What was revenue?", cl, "skim"))
#> Reading with 'skim' (all|N+1|none) over 5 chunk(s).
table(vapply(cl$calls(), function(x) x$label, character(1)))
#> 
#>  skim.answer skim.extract 
#>            1            5 

# A provider that is rate limited, then fails, then answers.
flaky <- hr_mock_client(mode = c(429, 500, 200))
vapply(1:3, function(i) hr_call(flaky, "hi")$ok, logical(1))
#> [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE
